sentences: Would you like to watch an experiment?
You must be patient.
Very patient.
This one started in 1927, and it is still going on today.
In 1927, Thomas Parnell, a professor in Brisbane, Australia, wanted to show his students something surprising.
Pitch is a black material.
It looks like a solid: you can break it with a hammer.
But Parnell said it was really a liquid — a very, very slow one.
He heated some pitch, put it in a glass funnel and waited.
The first drop fell in 1938.
The second fell in 1947.
Since 1927, only nine drops have fallen — about one drop every ten years.
Pitch flows billions of times more slowly than water.
Here is the strange part: nobody has ever seen a drop fall.
In 2000 a camera watched the funnel, but it stopped working at the wrong moment.
In 2014 the drop fell during a change of the glass.
Today the experiment has a webcam, and thousands of people watch it online.
The next drop is going to fall…
one day.
Maybe you will be the first person to see it.
Laura Dekker was born on a boat.
Her parents sailed around the world for seven years, and Laura was born in a port in New Zealand.
Her first home was the sea.
Maybe that is why, at thirteen, she made a big decision: she wanted to sail around the world alone.
Many people said no.
“She is too young,” they said.
“It is too dangerous.”
A court in the Netherlands stopped her for a year.
But Laura didn't give up.
She prepared her boat, Guppy, and she studied hard.
In August 2010, when she was fourteen, she finally left the port of Gibraltar.
The trip took more than a year.
Laura crossed the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean.
She saw dolphins, terrible storms and beautiful islands.
She was often alone for weeks.
She did her school homework on the boat and sent it by email.
In January 2012, Laura arrived in Sint Maarten, an island in the Caribbean.
She was sixteen.
Thousands of people met her at the port.
She was the youngest person in the world to sail around the planet alone.
“The sea was my teacher,” she said later.
It snowed all night in the village of Karagash.
In the morning, old Sabit went to his garden and stopped.
Ten apples were missing from his store.
There were footprints in the snow — big boots.
They went from the gate to the store, but they didn't come back.
They just stopped.
“Did the thief fly away?”
Sabit asked.
He called his granddaughter Ainur, who was twelve and loved detective books.
Ainur looked at the footprints closely.
“Grandpa,” she said, “these prints are deeper at the front.
And each print has two lines inside.”
Ainur smiled.
“The thief didn't fly.
He walked to the store, took the apples and walked back — backwards, in his own footprints.
That's why there are two lines.”
She followed the prints to the next house.
The neighbour's son, Marat, opened the door.
His boots were wet, and there was an apple in his hand.
“I'm sorry,” Marat said.
“I was going to bring them back.”
Sabit laughed.
“Next time, just ask.”
Ainur wrote in her notebook: The Footprints That Stopped.
Solved.
In 1969, workers near the village of Issyk, not far from Almaty, started to build a road.
They had to move an old hill.
But it was not a hill.
It was a kurgan — a grave from the time of the Saka people, more than two thousand years old.
Archaeologists came, and the leader was Kemal Akishev.
Inside, they found the skeleton of a young person, sixteen to eighteen years old, and about four thousand pieces of gold.
The clothes, the boots and the tall hat all had gold on them.
Scientists called the person “the Golden Man”.
There was also a silver cup with twenty-six strange signs.
Nobody has read them yet.
Some scientists think it is the oldest writing in Central Asia.
Others are not sure.
And there is one more question: was the Golden Man really a man?
Some archaeologists believe it was a young woman, a warrior princess.
Today the Golden Man is a symbol of Kazakhstan.
You can see him on the Independence Monument in Almaty, and copies of his clothes travel to museums around the world.
The workers finished the road too — a little later than they planned.
On 3 December 1992, a young engineer in England sat down at a computer and typed two words: “Merry Christmas”.
Then he pressed “send”.
Neil Papworth was twenty-two.
He didn't know that he had just made history.
The message went to a phone.
Richard Jarvis, a director at Vodafone, was at a Christmas party.
He read the two words on his big grey phone and smiled.
It was the first text message in the world.
Papworth didn't get an answer: in 1992 phones could receive texts, but they couldn't send them.
People had to write messages on a computer.
Why are text messages so short?
In 1985, a German engineer, Friedhelm Hillebrand, decided that 160 characters were enough for a message.
He typed many sentences on a typewriter and counted.
Most of them were shorter than 160 characters.
That rule has stayed for forty years.
Today people send billions of messages a day, but most of them go through apps, not SMS.
And that first “Merry Christmas”?
In 2021, Vodafone sold it as a digital object for more than one hundred thousand euros.
Not bad for two words.
Imagine a journey of 13,560 kilometres.
Now imagine it without food, without water and without a single stop.
A small bird did exactly that, and it was only five months old.
The bird was a bar-tailed godwit.
In October 2022, scientists put a tiny tag on its back in Alaska.
The tag sent signals to a satellite, so the scientists could follow the bird on their computers.
On 13 October the young godwit left Alaska and flew south over the Pacific Ocean.
It didn't land on any island.
It didn't eat any fish.
It flew day and night for eleven days.
On 24 October it landed in Tasmania, Australia.
That was a new world record for a bird flight without a stop.
How is this possible?
Before the journey, godwits eat and eat.
Fat is their fuel.
Then their bodies change: the stomach becomes smaller, and the heart and the flight muscles become bigger.
During the flight the bird loses about half of its weight.
Scientists still don't know if godwits sleep in the air.
And the young bird found the way alone — its parents didn't show it.
In 1979, a boy of sixteen walked along a river in India and saw something terrible.
After a big flood, hundreds of snakes lay dead on the hot sand — there were no trees and no shade.
Jadav Payeng cried.
Then he made a plan.
He came back with twenty small bamboo plants.
He planted them in the sand.
The next day he planted more.
And the next.
He carried water in pots.
He brought ants to make the soil better.
He did this every day — for forty years.
Today, the sand is a forest.
It is bigger than Central Park in New York.
Elephants, deer, rhinos and even tigers live there.
Birds come from far away.
Jadav still lives in a small house near the forest, and he still plants trees every morning.
People call him “the Forest Man of India”.
In 2015 he received one of the highest awards in the country.
“I didn't need help,” he says.
“I needed time.”
He is more than sixty, but he has a new dream: he is going to plant another forest.
He says he has enough time.
In March, the day and the night become the same length.
For people in Kazakhstan, 22 March is the beginning of the new year: Nauryz, “new day”.
The holiday is more than two thousand years old.
Before Nauryz, families clean their homes and pay their debts.
You should start the year with a clean house and a clean heart.
On the holiday, people put on traditional clothes and visit older relatives.
In the cities, yurts appear in the squares, and you can hear the dombra everywhere.
The most important food is Nauryz kozhe, a soup with seven ingredients: water, meat, salt, milk, grain and more.
Seven is a lucky number, so you must try seven bowls in seven houses — at least, that is what people say!
In the west of Kazakhstan, the holiday starts on 14 March.
This day is called Korisu, “the meeting day”.
In Soviet times, Nauryz was not an official holiday for many years.
It came back in 1988.
Since 2016, Nauryz in Kazakhstan has been on the UNESCO list of world heritage.
Today more than three hundred million people celebrate it.
Will you try seven bowls this year?
Every year, people take about half a million animals out of the sea, take some of their blood, and put them back.
The blood is blue.
And it has probably saved your life.
The animal is the horseshoe crab.
It looks like a small brown helmet with a long tail.
It is not really a crab — it is closer to spiders.
Horseshoe crabs have lived on Earth for 450 million years.
They are older than the dinosaurs, and they have not changed much.
Their blood is blue because it has copper in it, not iron like ours.
In the 1950s scientists discovered something amazing: when the blood meets dangerous bacteria, it becomes thick like jelly.
Today every new medicine and every vaccine must pass this blood test.
If the blood stays liquid, the medicine is clean.
Companies pay more than ten thousand dollars for a litre of blue blood.
Most crabs go back to the sea alive, but some die.
So scientists have made an artificial test, and laboratories are going to change to it.
The crabs have helped us for seventy years.
Now it is our turn to help them.
“It's only three hours,” said Daniyar.
“We'll be at the second lake before lunch.”
Aigerim wasn't sure: the sky was grey and the path was wet.
But they had a map on the phone, so they went.
The first hour was easy.
Then the path became narrower and steeper.
At a small river they saw two paths, and the phone showed the left one.
After another hour the path disappeared.
There were only trees, rocks and clouds.
The phone had no signal — and five per cent of battery.
“We must go back,” said Aigerim.
Then it started to rain.
Aigerim remembered a rule from her uncle, a mountain guide: if you are lost, don't go higher — go down to the water and follow it.
They found the river again and walked down beside it.
It was slow and cold, but the river knew the way.
Three hours later they saw a road and a man with a horse.
It was a ranger.
“The second lake?”
he laughed.
“It's on the other side of the mountain!”
They were wet and hungry, but safe.
The next morning they took the right path.
The lake was more beautiful than the photos.
In a library at Yale University in the USA, there is a book that nobody can read.
Not students, not professors, not the best code-breakers in the world.
People have tried for more than a hundred years.
The book has about 240 pages of animal skin from the years between 1404 and 1438.
The pages are full of small, neat letters, but they do not belong to any alphabet on Earth.
There are pictures too: strange plants that don't exist, stars, and women in green water.
A book dealer, Wilfrid Voynich, bought it in Italy in 1912.
That is why people call it “the Voynich manuscript”.
During the Second World War, the best code-breakers in America studied it.
They broke many secret codes, but not this one.
Computers have tried too.
Nothing works.
So what is it?
Some people think it is a secret language.
Others think a doctor wrote it for himself.
And some say it is a joke — a fake book from six hundred years ago.
Which is it?
You can look at every page online.
Maybe you should try.
Everyone else has failed.
On 14 March 1930, an eleven-year-old girl in Oxford, England, had breakfast with her grandfather.
He read the newspaper aloud: “They have found a new planet.
It is very far away and very cold.
But it has no name yet.”
Venetia Burney loved stories about Greek and Roman gods.
She thought for a moment.
“Why not call it Pluto?”
she said.
Pluto was the god of the dark world under the ground.
It was a good name for a dark, cold planet.
Her grandfather liked the idea.
He told an astronomer at Oxford University, and the astronomer sent a telegram to the USA, to the scientists who found the planet.
They had hundreds of ideas, but they chose Venetia's.
On 1 May 1930 the planet officially became Pluto.
Venetia got five pounds as a prize.
Venetia became a teacher and lived to ninety.
In 2006 scientists decided that Pluto was too small for a “real” planet and called it a dwarf planet.
“It's still Pluto,” Venetia said.
In 2015 a spacecraft flew past Pluto for the first time.
On board there was an instrument with her name.
When you send a photo to a friend in another country, it doesn't fly through the air.
It goes down.
More than 99 per cent of the data between countries travels through cables at the bottom of the sea.
There are more than five hundred of these cables, about 1.
4 million kilometres in total — enough to go around the Earth thirty-five times.
In the deep sea a cable is not much thicker than a garden hose.
Inside, the data travels as light through thin glass fibres.
The idea is old.
In 1858 engineers laid the first cable across the Atlantic Ocean.
The Queen of England sent a message to the President of the USA: it was short, but it took sixteen hours to arrive.
Three weeks later the cable stopped working.
In 1866 a new cable worked for years.
Cables break, of course.
Ships' anchors and fishing nets cause most problems, and sometimes a shark bites one.
Special ships find the broken cable, lift it from the sea floor and repair it.
So when your video call is slow, remember: your words are travelling through the dark water, thousands of metres down.
In the mountains of Utah, USA, there is a forest of about forty-seven thousand trees.
They have white bark and small round leaves.
In autumn they all turn yellow on the same day.
Why?
Because they are not forty-seven thousand trees.
They are one tree.
The forest is called Pando, which means “I spread” in Latin.
Every tree grows from the same roots under the ground.
Scientists tested the leaves, and all of them have exactly the same DNA.
Above the ground, Pando looks like a forest.
Below, it is one enormous living thing.
Pando covers forty-three hectares, about sixty football fields, and weighs about six thousand tonnes — heavier than any whale.
Scientists think it has lived for thousands of years.
The trunks die and new ones grow, but the roots continue.
Pando has a problem.
Deer and cows eat almost all the young trunks, so the forest is getting older.
People have built fences around parts of Pando, and there new trees are growing.
“Pando is the biggest living thing we know,” says one scientist, “and we should not lose it.”
When Bolat Ata turned seventy, his family gave him a present: a big soft armchair.
“Now you can rest,” they said.
Bolat Ata looked at the chair, then out of the window.
The next morning at six o'clock he put on his old sports shoes and went out.
At first he couldn't run for two minutes.
His legs hurt, and his neighbours laughed.
“Where are you going, Ata?”
“To the shop,” he said.
But he went to the park every day and ran a little further: one kilometre, then three, then five.
His granddaughter Aliya found out after a month.
She didn't laugh.
She bought him new shoes and made a plan.
“Ata, the Almaty Marathon is in April,” she said.
“The short race is ten kilometres.
You should try.”
“I'm going to run it faster than you,” he said.
In April, thousands of people ran the Almaty Marathon.
Bolat Ata was the oldest runner in his group, but not the slowest.
When he crossed the finish line, the whole family was there — with the armchair.
“Now you can rest,” they said.
He sat down for one minute.
Then he got up.
“Next year, the half marathon,” he said.
Thimphu is a capital city with cars, shops, offices and about one hundred thousand people.
But it has something that no other capital in the world has: no traffic lights.
Not one.
Bhutan is a small country in the Himalayas.
Years ago, the city put one traffic light on the main street, but people didn't like it.
“It's too impersonal,” they said, and the city took it away.
Today police officers in white gloves direct the cars with their hands.
Drivers say it is more polite than a machine.
Bhutan is different in other ways too.
Television and the internet arrived only in 1999.
The country doesn't measure success in money.
In the 1970s the king said that “Gross National Happiness” was more important than money.
So the government asks people about their health, their free time and their friends.
The law says that more than sixty per cent of the country must always be forest.
Bhutan takes more carbon out of the air than it puts in.
Tourists must pay a fee for every day of their visit.
It is expensive, but the roads are quiet, the air is clean, and you will never wait at a red light.
